messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 23
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Auditor
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 58

**Vignette: Priya**

Priya is a 23-year-old South Asian woman who works as a junior auditor at a mid-sized accounting firm in the city. She is precise by nature, someone who has always found comfort in numbers and order — in the reassurance that columns balance and that the world, when examined carefully enough, makes sense. That belief was shattered two years ago, and she has not fully recovered it since.

Priya was visiting extended family in her parents' home country when the conflict escalated without warning. What began as a two-week trip to attend a cousin's wedding became something else entirely. She was in the family home when the shelling started in a neighboring district. Over the following eleven days, she witnessed things she had no framework to absorb: a market she had walked through reduced to rubble overnight, a neighbor carried out of a collapsed building, the sound of aircraft that made everyone around her drop to the floor without thinking. She was never physically injured, a fact she returns to often, as though it should mean she has no right to what she carries. She eventually evacuated through a crowded border crossing, separated briefly from her aunt in the chaos, certain for forty minutes that she would not make it out.

She returned to her job three weeks later, telling herself that work would anchor her. In many ways, it has — and in many ways, it has complicated everything. Auditing requires sustained concentration, the ability to hold sequences of information in mind and trace them forward and backward through time. Priya now finds that concentration fractures unpredictably. She will be reviewing a financial statement and a sound from the open-plan office — a door slamming, a raised voice from a nearby meeting room — will pull her out of the present entirely. Her heart accelerates. Her hands go cold. For several seconds she is not at her desk but somewhere else, crouched beside a window with the curtains drawn, listening. Her colleagues have noticed that she startles easily and have begun to treat her with a careful quietness she finds both kind and suffocating.

Sleep is where the worst of it lives. Priya wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, her body already in full alert before she is conscious of why. The dreams are not always dramatic — sometimes she simply dreams of the border crossing, the press of people, the noise, the forty minutes without her aunt — and wakes with the same terror as if the building were falling. She has taken to leaving the television on low all night, which helps marginally and exhausts her completely.

She does not talk about any of this at work. She does not talk about it much anywhere. Her parents know she was frightened during the trip but do not know the extent of what she saw, and she has chosen not to tell them, partly to protect them and partly because she does not trust herself to speak about it without losing composure in a way that feels unbearable to her. She is the daughter who is doing well, who has a professional job in a good city, and she is not ready to revise that story.

What troubles her most, she says quietly in session, is not the nightmares or even the startle responses — it is the flatness that has settled over things she used to love. She used to call her grandmother every Sunday and talk for an hour. Now she lets the calls go to voicemail and feels guilty about it for days. She used to find genuine pleasure in a well-constructed audit trail. Now she finishes her work and feels nothing in particular. She describes it as living behind glass — able to see her own life clearly, able to perform it competently, but unable to quite touch it. She is 23 years old and she is already tired in a way she does not have words for yet.
